underline;">OWID</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A data point that gets thrown around a lot is that the UK is as poor as Mississippi. In GDP (PPP) terms, that’s true — Mississippi’s income per capita is about $56,000, roughly similar to the UK. That doesn’t mean life is equally as good in the two countries — Mississippi is more violent and less healthy than Britain. But unless you think that Britain had to sacrifice a significant portion of its material wealth in order to be safer and healthier, this is a bit beside the point. France and Germany, which are just as safe and healthy as the UK (if not more so), </span><em>also</em><span> have significantly higher incomes. This is from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f2600333-dba9-4752-b792-577051f48afb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a Resolution Foundation report</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Middle-income Brits are now 20 per cent poorer than their peers in Germany and 9 per cent poorer than those in France. Worse, low-income households in the UK are now around 27 per cent poorer than their French and German counterparts. It’s important to comprehend just how material these gaps are: the living standards of the lowest-income households in the UK are £4,300 lower than their French equivalents.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A very deep principle in economics is that if two countries are roughly equivalent in terms of their basic institutions, they ought to converge to similar income levels. The fact that the UK and the U.S. have diverged rather than converged suggests that the former must have some institutional weaknesses relative to the latter. And that implies that there are cautionary tales here for America. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What are those cautionary tales? There are a number of good breakdowns of the UK’s problems, and you can learn a lot from observing the overlaps and disagreements between them. Ben Southwood, Samuel Hughes, and Sam Bowman have a long piece called “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/016f62c0-d0e5-4f86-a4ec-888eec2e689f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Foundations</a><span>”, which basically makes a libertarian YIMBY argument; they claim the UK is over-regulated and can’t build housing, infrastructure, or really anything else. Jim Tomlinson has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/800cb1d0-c9de-4e4c-85d2-570a083defe2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a rebuttal</a><span> in which he argues that the real barrier to investment is the financialization of the UK economy. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/18cd15db-d365-45b7-903c-a7aed35362d1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Ben Ansell argues</a><span> that the UK is in a version of the “high-level equilibrium trap” — the UK is still fairly wealthy, so its politics center around how to divide up the pie rather than growing it. The Resolution Foundation’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f2600333-dba9-4752-b792-577051f48afb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">report</a><span> has lots of suggestions for how to get Britain growing again. Michelle Kilfoyle also has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8c0432e1-a8d8-4731-b036-36b1f46ab96a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">some recommendations</a><span>. These are only a few examples.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But my favorite rundown is probably </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bdec967f-b1ac-4a33-9968-e4ca18257346?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the recent </a><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bdec967f-b1ac-4a33-9968-e4ca18257346?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Atlantic</a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bdec967f-b1ac-4a33-9968-e4ca18257346?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"> article</a><span> by Idrees Kahloon. The article points out that it isn’t </span><em>just</em><span> private industry that’s broken in the UK; it’s also the effectiveness of the government institutions that many British people cherish. This includes the fabled National Health Service. Kahloon writes:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Taxation is at the highest level since World War II, yet public services have deteriorated. The National Health Service, the celebrated pillar of the British cradle-to-grave welfare state, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/86d7a424-853d-4f87-a2ec-86866c623902?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">has a backlog of 6 million patients</a><span>—almost a tenth of the population—waiting for treatment. The health service now has to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f102c6ae-687f-4842-9785-51c361e00a16?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">spend more money settling maternity-malpractice claims</a><span> than it does on actually providing maternity care. Many Brits can neither obtain an appointment with a publicly funded dentist nor afford a private one; in a 2023 survey, one in 10 reported doing DIY dental work, in extreme cases extracting their own teeth or gluing broken crowns back together…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Incomes can be shockingly low: Junior doctors recently went on strike for the 15th time in three years over their salaries, which start at just £38,800; the median salary for British civil servants is £35,680…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Recent plans to transform the country['s transportation system] have rested in no small part on High Speed 2, a superfast rail line intended to connect London with Birmingham, Leeds, and Manchester. But since HS2 was proposed, in 2009, its costs have tripled, to more than £100 billion. It is the most expensive rail line in the world. (A special structure to protect a rare bat species near the rail line in Buckinghamshire required 8,000 permits and was built at a cost of £216 million.) The most important sections of the proposed route have been lopped off. The rump line—going from Birmingham, Britain’s second-largest city, to not-quite-central London—may be finished by 2040…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Building infrastructure, or much of anything else, has become all but impossible in the United Kingdom. In addition to having the world’s most expensive (not yet built) train line, Britain also hosts the world’s most expensive (not yet built) nuclear-power plant, Hinkley Point C. Its environmental-impact assessment ran 31,401 pages; the plant will feature a £700 million “fish disco,” which will pulse sounds underwater to deter animals from its intake pipes. The government spent 32 years and £179 million planning a tunnel beneath Stonehenge to relieve traffic, only to officially scrap the plan this year. Even basic tasks, such as obtaining power, can be nightmarish…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Britain suffers from a housing crisis significantly worse than America’s. The problem cannot even be blamed on zoning, because Britain does not have a zoning regime to speak of. Rather, every attempt to build is a painful, ad hoc negotiation with local government councils and NIMBY residents. As a result, housing costs per square foot are among the highest in Europe. In </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f2646ae1-51de-4be2-a719-f9538f9a85a2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the words of one report</a><span>, “Our housing stock offers the worst value for money of any advanced economy.” France has roughly the same population as the U.K., but almost 50 percent more homes. And yet, since the financial crisis, the U.K.’s rate of housing production has only fallen…In London, the typical house sold in 2024 cost 11 times median earnings.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One of the key lessons here appears to be that </span><strong>NIMBYism kills the economy by a thousand small cuts</strong><span>. But Americans already know this. Kahloon’s description of Britain’s struggle to build high speed rail sounds uncomfortably like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4c958b7e-3c07-4deb-ae7c-8fb8c019806c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">California’s story</a><span>. And the housing story is also very similar to America’s. Most of the other analyses I listed above identify NIMBY-driven housing scarcity as one of the key factors holding back growth in the UK, and recommend various different strategies to address it. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’m not sure the U.S. has a lot to learn from those various proposals, since they’re highly specific to the UK’s institutional context. But the overall lessons here are worth reiterating: Approval policies full of veto points and cumbersome procedures are a drag on the economy, local control can easily go too far, good infrastructure is often a matter of low-cost efficiency rather than pure willingness to pay, and so on. Americans have a severe NIMBY problem, but they can look over at the UK as a cautionary tale of how bad things will get if the NIMBY problem is allowed to fester.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another lesson that Americans have already learned is </span><strong>the peril of excessive financialization</strong><span> of the economy. Almost everyone agrees that the UK economy is excessively concentrated in London. John Burn-Murdoch </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/00438f2e-f928-42df-b8ff-4eafe9645c63?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">writes</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It will surprise nobody that London accounts for an outsized share of Britain’s output, but the magnitude of the UK’s economic monopolarity is remarkable. Removing London’s output and headcount would shave 14 per cent off British living standards, precisely enough to slip behind the last of the US states. Britain in the aggregate may not be as poor as Mississippi, but absent its outlier capital it would be.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Not only does this mean that the fruits of the UK economy are inequitably distributed — requiring a constant stream of politically difficult transfers to keep other regions afloat — but it also means that NIMBYism bites much harder than it otherwise would, because pricing people out of London means pricing them out of participation in one of the few healthy parts of Britain’s economy, and because pricing people out of highly productive cities hurts productivity. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And part of the reason the UK’s economy clusters in London is </span><em>finance</em><span>. As Reuters reports, the UK economy </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73edf415-4260-405f-9112-dddfef43f56b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">specializes in finance</a><span>: </span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The United Kingdom is unusually dependent on finance. Financial services account for about 12% of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f742aac5-d8ca-47cf-b9ea-a9ec74876047?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>economic output</span><span>, opens new tab</span></a><span>, compared with around 7% in the United States. Much of that activity emanates from London. The City is the world’s second-largest asset management hub, the leading venue for foreign exchange trading, and the number one location for over-the-counter derivatives.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Finance is an industry with an especially strong </span><em>clustering effect</em><span>; almost every country has just one city that’s the “financial capital” — NYC in the U.S., Tokyo in Japan, etc. But in an economy as financialized as Britain’s, the financial capital is the center of the entire economy, probably to an unhealthy degree.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another obvious downside of financialization is that specialization in a single tentpole industry made the UK economy unusually vulnerable to a crash in that industry. The financial crisis of 2008, and the follow-on Euro Crisis in the years afterward, dealt a heavy blow to the UK finance industry — and, thus, to the UK economy. Whether you think Britain’s GDP stagnation truly began in 2008 or 2016, it’s inarguable that real wages </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9c765826-2c71-48da-80f7-a49818915ff7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">stagnated and fell for years</a><span> after 2008. Compare average weekly earnings in the UK to those in the U.S., and the difference is crystal clear:</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" none;">shortages</a><span>, etc. — isn’t clear. But just these two negative effects — the UK economy’s hyper-concentration in London, and its vulnerability to single-sector shocks — provide a cautionary tale about letting an economy rely too much on the finance industry. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Again, this is a lesson that Americans already learned, at least partially, after 2008 (though thankfully, the lesson was somewhat less painful for us than for the Brits). But one lesson from 2008 that the U.S. should pay attention to is that </span><strong>fiscal austerity</strong><span>, if done too abruptly and carelessly, </span><strong>can leave long-term scars</strong><span> on an economy. Kahloon writes:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">[T]he government’s actions during and after the [2008] crisis compounded the damage. Rather than increase spending to revive depressed demand, as modern Keynesians would counsel, the government…opted to slash budgets as revenue plunged…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Funding for day-to-day NHS operations was maintained, for instance, but only by cannibalizing the capital budget. A </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f199f882-c93d-4c28-804b-02360e496235?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">2024 government report found</a><span> that, as a result of austerity, Britain has “crumbling buildings, mental health patients being accommodated in Victoria-era cells infested with vermin with 17 men sharing two showers, and parts of the NHS operating in decrepit portacabins.”…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After austerity cuts to welfare benefits took effect, the share of children who grew up in long-term poverty, meaning half their childhood or more, shot up </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fce919ec-7526-44ad-8d59-c00debc6b16b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">from about 14 percent to 23 percent</a><span>. Nutrition appeared to suffer, and doctors reported increased cases of diseases stemming from vitamin deficiencies, such as rickets and scurvy.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The U.S. needs to hear this lesson. 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’re going to need to do fiscal austerity, but it’s important that we do it gradually, by restraining the </span><em>growth </em><span>of spending (and raising taxes), rather than by abruptly slashing government services and public works.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Kahloon’s example of the NHS actually demonstrates another lesson — the UK’s strategy of providing health care is probably uniquely flawed. In most advanced countries, the government provides universal health </span><em>insurance</em><span>; the government pays part of the cost of health care, but it doesn’t actually provide the care directly. The UK government, in contrast, provides health care directly to its people as a state-owned enterprise. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Britain’s NHS helps control costs in the short term; the system is cheaper than those of other rich countries, for roughly similar outcomes. But in the long term, it makes the UK’s health system subject to the whims and vagaries of politics. After the 2008 crisis, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0354d36d-afb6-448a-a7d2-5a0ddde85ead?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the UK disinvested severely</a><span> from health care because of fiscal austerity policy, while other countries continued to do the necessary capital spending to maintain future services. This is a big part of the reason why the NHS system is now </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7b1e892b-a08e-4f77-b097-b9f75bc4e8e2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">widely seen as falling apart</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The U.S. is vanishingly unlikely to switch to nationalized, state-run health care provision — at the very most, we’ll get a system of national </span><em>insurance</em><span>, like most other rich countries have. But watching the degradation of the NHS should remind us of why </span><strong>direct government provision of necessary services is so dangerous</strong><span>. It’s not necessarily that government is inherently inefficient; it’s that it’s inherently </span><em>political</em><span>. UK-style austerity is one reason government can starve its own enterprises of capital spending, but it’s not the only one — under Hugo Chavez, Veneuzela’s government </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3fe20aca-e0df-4720-a9cd-66f2b13711f2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">starved its own state-owned oil company</a><span> of capital investment in order to deliver a bonanza of government largesse, with predictably disastrous results. We should remember this when socialists like Zohran Mamdani </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ba1fe6a9-b0b6-4068-a476-8bc5f6ba7f59?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">promise</a><span> to run essential services through the government. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One key lesson that all the analyses of Britain’s troubles seem to already have internalized, but which the U.S. needs to pay attention to, is that </span><strong>maintaining overseas markets is very important</strong><span>. Whether 2008 caused a long-term economic slowdown or not, 2016 definitely seems to have done so. Brexit is the huge, looming shadow that hangs over everything that has happened to the UK economy over the past decade.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2795fff2-fa57-4a87-a8af-fbea837ecbb6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Bloom et al. (2025)</a><span> study the growth impact of Brexit, looking at both macro data and micro data. For the macro, they assume Brexit was an unanticipated shock, and compare the UK to other countries. For the micro, they look at how various British businesses fare after Brexit, according to how dependent they were on the EU before the big surprise breakup. Both estimates agree that Brexit was a negative shock:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">[B]y the end of 2025 Brexit had reduced UK GDP by 6% to 8%, with the impact accumulating steadily over time. We estimate that investment was reduced by 12% to 13%, employment by 3% to 4% and productivity by 3% to 4%. These negative impacts reflect a combination of elevated uncertainty, reduced demand, diverted management time, and increased misallocation of resources from a protracted Brexit process.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2227390d-8526-4eb1-9f5a-2f6a887250c5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Other</a><span> studies </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2332370e-99e3-48f8-9f8c-89a2c335334b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">agree</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The U.S. should look at Britain’s experience and remember that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/43b7e22a-cbae-4f7b-8223-db97c16b0385?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">international markets matter</a><span>. The pre-Brexit UK was a more internationalized economy than the pre-Trump U.S. — exports are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2f72e830-4191-4c91-bcaa-0abf1f68d21a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">over 30% of UK GDP</a><span>, compared to only 11% in the U.S. But that seemingly small stream of exports revenues supports a lot of more local industries, through the magic of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/839d0ae0-4031-41b4-a515-d5c2ead24a01?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">local multiplier effects</a><span>. If Trump and his successors disrupt those markets by starting pointless trade wars with allies and friendly countries, the results won’t be quite as bad as in the UK, but they won’t be good.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A final lesson that the UK’s failures can teach the U.S. is that </span><strong>energy supply is very important</strong><span>. Most analyses tend to gloss over the chronic energy scarcity that has afflicted the UK in recent years. “Foundations”, however, puts this squarely in the limelight:</span></p><div Pix, a digital payment system, almost 6 years ago. The system </span><span>— which allows people to make payments on their phones, not very differently from Apple Pay or Google Pay, except that Pix payments are official currency rather than transfers from private companies</span><span> — has been highly successful. The vast majority of Brazilians use it regularly, and by all accounts Pix — which is free for individuals, and cheap for businesses — is hugely popular.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On Wednesday — as it happens, on the first anniversary of an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7b31068e-9dfd-4bd2-9bc3-e562fb901e5d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">article</a><span> I posted praising Pix and suggesting that it may represent the future of money — the Trump administration will try to punish Brazil for this success. It will do so by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0c51a39d-eaec-4f7e-abe9-29a054aad8ed?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">imposing tariffs</a><span> on Brazilian exports under </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0fd4e8a1-1bb0-4312-bbc8-ea806dfb838e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Section 301</a><span> of the 1974 Trade Act, which permits such tariffs to counter “unfair trade practices.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why is it unfair for a nation to offer its own citizens a better way to make purchases and pay bills? To some extent the Trump administration is still trying to punish Brazil for being a real democracy.</span><span> Unlike the United States, Brazil put its former president, Jair Bolsonaro, on trial for trying to foment an insurrection when he lost the last election</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Trump’s hostility towards Brazil’s Pix system is also </span><span>an illustration of the same phenomenon we see in </span><span>his </span><span>energy policy: this administration is hostile to progress whenever that progress works against the interests and ideology of the oligarchs who have poured money into Trump’s campaigns and his pockets.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pix is essentially a digital version of the </span><em><span>real</span></em><span>, Brazil’s currency. As a Federal Reserve </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ad150074-2ba0-48a7-a890-92eaa075d742?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>report</span></a><span> from 2022 said, a central bank digital currency — which is what Pix is — “is analogous to a digital form of paper money.” Brazilian banks are required to offer Pix, which the Trumpists claim gives it an unfair advantage over debit cards and other payment methods. But this requirement is similar, at a fundamental level, to the requirement that all U.S. banks accept dollar notes as deposits and disburse dollar notes on demand, which few people would consider unfair.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Who</span><span> is hurt by the advent of Pix</span><span>? Brazilians’ ability to cheaply make instantaneous payments from their phones certainly hurts the business of Visa and Mastercard, which are both U.S. companies. But since when is it unfair </span><span>business practice </span><span>when companies lose business to a competitor that offers a better, cheaper product?</span><span> For example, should we shut down the U.S. postal service because it offers better and cheaper mail delivery than UPS or FedEx? Should we shut down PayPal and Venmo because they compete with Mastercard and Visa?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Beyond concerns about Visa and Mastercard profits, Trump officials are reportedly concerned that Pix and similar payment systems elsewhere might challenge the international dominance of the dollar. In reality, Brazil is too small a player to make much of a dent in the world payments system. The dollar may, however, face a real challenge if the European Central Bank is able, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/505266e6-81b7-4373-be9e-367499894734?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">as it hopes</a><span>, to introduce a digital euro in 2029. If that happens, it’s not hard to imagine that a significant number of transactions that would otherwise have been made in dollars will be made in digital euros instead.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But let’s be clear: the reason people might switch to digital euros will be because the US won’t be offering a</span><span>n equally good</span><span> means of payment. Why won’t there be a digital dollar? Not because it’s a bad idea — as Brazil has shown, it would be a very good idea. But there are powerful special interests that oppose any such move.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Last year Republicans in the House passed a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f8f01507-b48d-41e5-bea9-82ea11fc9c7a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">bill</a><span> that didn’t just forbid the creation of a U.S. central bank digital currency; it prohibited any study of the issue by the Federal Reserve. “Don’t even </span><em>think</em><span> about </span><s>parking here</s><span> creating a digital dollar.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Proponents of this ban claimed to have concerns about how a central bank digital currency would work. But it’s obvious that their real concern is that it would work too well. Crypto interests, in particular, are very worried that consumers who had access to digital dollars would lose interest in stablecoins and other cryptocurrency products, because these products, being risky and awkward to use, would not be competitive with a system that simply lets people make electronic payments in dollars.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Brazil’s success is especially galling to crypto promoters because it’s in such stark contrast to the results of another Latin American monetary experiment: El Salvador’s attempt to make Bitcoin a major means of payment. The government of President Nayib Bukele made Bitcoin legal tender and spent large sums trying to promote its use. Yet the effort </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d6b62c06-dcd8-451e-bc6c-2493d3a3ef54?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">failed</a><span>: cryptocurrency never caught on as a means of payment, and the plunge in Bitcoin’s price since last fall has inflicted large losses on El Salvador’s government.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Beyond special-interest opposition, Brazil’s digital currency clearly raises the ire of right-wingers who hate the idea of a government providing a service that could have been offered by the private sector, even — or rather especially — if the government can do it better. If we can have a digital dollar, why not a public option for health insurance?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Finally, the furious opposition to central bank digital currencies reminds me of the Trump administration’s all-out efforts to block development of wind and solar power. In both cases we see political players beholden to special interests — crypto when it comes to money, fossil fuels when it comes to energy — who claim to favor technological progress, but scream “not like that” when a superior technology doesn’t take the economy where they want it to go.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, using tariffs to punish Brazil for its monetary achievements won’t succeed. Politically, the move will only strengthen Brazil’s President Lula. Economically, the reach of the tariffs will be limited by Trump administration fears about driving the prices of coffee, orange juice, beef and other goods even higher. And as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/121c63ec-6d1b-4796-a5e5-32c261425e42?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Monica de Bolle</a><span> at the Peterson Institute for International Economics argues, Trump’s tariffs have on balance strengthened Brazil’s position: “</span><span>Trade diversion around the globe as a reaction to US tariffs has turned Brazil into an export powerhouse,” with Brazil, for example, capturing much of the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0ba106f1-c4b9-40b7-b0f6-0ac13db9b5eb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Chinese soybean market</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the obvious folly of these new tariffs won’t stop them from happening. The Trump administration has declared war on the future — and one thing we know about Trump is that he never admits it when his wars of choice fail.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MUSICAL CODA</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I know, they’re Catalan, but I really like this</span></p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/86e81563-2578-4f8d-ac1d-ed490f9cc329?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/z9Qe6HIxPxc" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><span>Former U.S. Senate candidate Graham Platner speaks during a campaign event with the Maine A.F.L.-C.I.O. on May 1, 2026, in Portland, Maine. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2d44aa29-e277-492d-8aa8-9658af31738e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Graeme Sloan</a><span>/Stringer via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The implosion of Graham Platner’s Senate campaign has spurred an interesting discussion of class in America. I think there are two reasons this episode is revealing, both of which stem from the Platner campaign’s decision to characterize him as a working-class candidate with working-class appeal. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One reason is that while Platner is unambiguously “working class” in the sense that he “does not have a college degree,” he’s an odd fit for the role in a lot of other ways. He’s a small-business owner whose mom also owns a small business and whose dad is a successful country lawyer. He went to private high schools and to George Washington University in D.C. Yes, he dropped out of G.W. and thus qualifies as a non-college person — which really is how political demographers characterize the working class — but does this actually make sense? </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When I first started working in political journalism, I found the idea of a definition of working class that included Bill Gates (at the time the richest man in the world) somewhat absurd. But I was beaten down by convention and have generally used the term the way everyone else does. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The Platner experience, though, puts this question back on the table. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The other reason is that while Platner had a good chance of beating Susan Collins before being derailed by scandal, there was no evidence that he was beating benchmarks in appealing to non-college voters. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Zohran Mamdani’s strength in the New York City mayoral race was with younger and better-educated voters. In Michigan, Haley Stevens is winning with non-college voters while Abdul El-Sayed is dominating with better-educated ones. You even see this internal to labor unions. The current leadership of the United Auto Workers is a left-wing faction within the union that was able to prevail in the most recent internal election largely thanks to the strength of unionized graduate-student instructors rather than people who work in the auto industry. It’s just clearly true that the audience for left-wing politics is primarily college graduates. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One way of squaring both of these circles is to adopt a line that Platner himself used in an interview: The working class is anyone who works for a living. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“My definition of working class these days is essentially anybody who makes money from wages,” </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3ae4df42-0122-4790-bb4c-6eff60a9b89c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">he told the New York Times in May</a><span>. “If you work for a living and you go out and put in hours and you pay taxes just like everyone else, I think that’s quite fair.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When I first saw he said that, I thought it was idiosyncratic. But over the past couple of months, it’s become clear this definition appeals to a lot of people. It helpfully squares the circle — the kinds of left-wing people who are most inclined to talk about working-class politics tend to be college-educated professionals, and they naturally want to define the adherents of their own movement as working class. And it makes semantic sense. What is the “working” in “working class” if not a reference to the fact that people are working for a living? </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This definition of working class is so expansive that it’s not actually useful, though. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The idea of “class” is an important part of our social and cultural legacy. It’s obviously a critical concept in Karl Marx’s work, and Marx exerts a large influence over all kinds of left-wing social analysis. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s also a real and prominent feature of 18th- and 19th-century British and European societies, and all kinds of non-leftist literary and historical works that constitute our shared heritage invoke it all the time. But I think the more you try to make these ideas work in characterizing the contemporary United States, the more it looks like a mirage. We have a lot of inequality in this country, but we don’t have much in the way of sharply discontinuous social classes.  </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Traditional “class” analysis is discontinuous </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you open a book by Jane Austen or a novel such as George Eliot’s “Middlemarch,” you’ll find portrayals of English social class in the first half of the 19th century. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And a key feature of the society depicted in these works is that while there is a degree of social mobility, both upward and downward, there are also real boundary conditions around class. England had a titled aristocracy with formal membership rules. You’re either in that class or you’re not! It also had a gentry class, composed of the owners of large estates who made a living by renting out land to tenant farmers. The tenant farmers were a different class — lumped together with the servants who’d be employed by the gentry. Between the tenant farmers and the gentry were a “middle class” of professionals and also a group of yeoman farmers who owned their own land. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And over the course of the 19th century, these arrangements were perturbed by the Industrial Revolution. A new class of rich people owned factories and a new “working class” of urban laborers worked in the factories. Importantly, though, as your English teachers would no doubt be at pains to point out, while money was very important, class was still somewhat distinct in these settings. Making a lot of money in trade or manufacturing did not make you a gentleman. And affluent tradespeople would often try to buy a country estate and have their kids or grandkids assimilate into gentry status.  </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is just to say that while it’s not that you </span><em>couldn’t</em><span> cross the boundaries from one social class to another, there was a bit of a taboo around it. There was a difference between being a real country squire and a guy who bought an estate yesterday. And people looked at least a little bit askance at folks who worked their way up the ladder. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You clearly see in the Platner story, though, that there’s just nothing like </span><em>that</em><span> in America. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When people say that Elon Musk’s dad owned an emerald mine, that’s meant as a knock on Musk. In America, we diminish people’s achievements by saying they came from affluent families who gave them a leg up. And it’s normal to accuse people of painting an exaggerated portrait of hardscrabble origins. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Michael Kinsley wrote a great piece 25 years ago about the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a883adfe-f592-40b5-8da9-ce2c5944f8ab?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">prominence of reverse snobbery in American life</a><span> that has, if anything, only become more prevalent. We just don’t have discontinuous social classes the way you’d find in Austen books or while watching or reading “Game of Thrones.” It does not make sense in our society for a kid with rich parents to try to make himself look better by obscuring the fact that his parents earned their money rather than inherited it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the Marxist idea that how people relate to the means of production is important still makes a lot of sense. It’s just that here, too, we don’t have a sharp categorical divide. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">America’s mixed bourgeois society</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The Marxist idea was that industrial capitalism would end up looking a lot like feudal agriculture. Instead of landlords and tenants (or nobles and peasants), you’d have bourgeois people who own the means of production and a proletarian class of people who work for a living. And clearly this dynamic does exist in the United States today. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Walmart is the largest private-sector employer in America, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/594a435b-d076-4a8f-9fde-469c7b706da8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">seven of the 400 richest people in America are heirs</a><span> to the Walmart fortune. Walmart, of course, employs all kinds of people, but the largest segment of its workforce is rank-and-file folks making low wages. It’s not exactly the same as a factory in 1876, but the dynamic is broadly similar: You have people who own shares of stock in the company, and you have people working for the company. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But while these poles exist, they exist in a context in which most people are somewhat between them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m sure the guy who actually </span><em>runs</em><span> Walmart, C.E.O. John Furner, owns many shares of Walmart stock. But he didn’t inherit them. He started out </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/28bf2b09-3e05-46ec-b361-d70487abfb33?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">stocking shelves at a Walmart retail location in Bentonville</a><span>, went to the University of Arkansas, moved on to the company’s management track after graduating, and apparently did well and became C.E.O.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That’s obviously an unusual life trajectory. But it’s true that most established companies are run by a set of executives whose financial interests are aligned with shareholders via stock options but who are also definitely “working for a living.” </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And while coming all the way up from stocking shelves is unusual, you do normally get to be C.E.O. by doing a lot of lower-status jobs first. Tim Cook </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dd3bdf98-504d-4767-a163-1bc68ffadb18?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">worked</a><span> for 12 years at IBM, became C.O.O. of the computer reselling division of a company called Intelligent Electronics, and then was an executive at Compaq when Steve Jobs </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/723b7148-fb0d-4601-9ee3-faf784afe19f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">hired him</a><span> in 1998 to become Apple’s senior vice president of worldwide operations. From there he was promoted two or three more times and eventually became C.E.O. of the world’s most valuable company. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s not just that there’s something illogical about characterizing rich executives like Furner and Cook as “working class” — it defies the actual economics of the situation. The executives are definitely working for a living, but they are receiving all this stock-based compensation to make sure their economic interests are fully aligned with the owners. </p><div style="text-decoration: none;">Subscribed</span></a></div></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But who are the owners? </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With Walmart, the Walton family is by far the largest shareholder. But the largest shareholders in Apple are just investment funds like Vanguard and BlackRock. About </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c2bc574b-33fe-4add-b8c4-9ddf88bdc1f5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">65 percent</a><span> of the company’s shares are owned by E.T.F.s and mutual funds. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Which is to say it’s not even like there’s some Richie Rich owner pulling the strings behind Cook. He, as C.E.O., is the pointy end of the spear of the interests of capital. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But capital in this case is largely random retirement accounts. Most very rich people work for their daily bread, and most working people own at least some capital. More than </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/47df6882-65fc-458a-8d99-130d22580cbf?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">60 percent of Americans own shares of stock</a><span>, and a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6c370aed-a1e6-493e-b5e3-876e62891660?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">comparable share of households own a home</a><span>. These are also partially life-cycle effects. You have young people who own neither stock nor homes but who realistically will later in life — only 44 percent of people under 30 own stock, for example. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s also a big </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/47df6882-65fc-458a-8d99-130d22580cbf?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">education gradient</a><span>. More than 80 percent of college graduates own shares, as do 87 percent of people with incomes over $100,000. People with lower earnings and less education are less likely to own stock. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s not that you would look at Jane, who works in the accounting department and has a 401(k), and John, the C.F.O., and say, “They’re just the same. They both have jobs and they both own stock.” These are different economic situations. But the American economy is a spectrum, to say nothing of the very large share of people who don’t work for for-profit enterprises. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Workers without capitalists</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is, I think, a very underrated divide in terms of Americans’ relationships to the means of production. About </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0cdb5726-67ce-4606-869b-3bca98ca3819?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">15 percent</a><span> of the labor force works for some level of the government. Another </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7b83aad3-3996-4a3f-bf05-689e317583d9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">10 percent</a><span> work for nonprofits, mostly in health care. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">These jobs feature distinctions of pay, job function, and status, but they don’t feature literal clashes between workers and owners because there are no owners. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One reason this distinction is important is that labor unions, which are very important in the political rhetoric of class, are much more prevalent in the government sector than in private business. Concurrently, a large share of recent labor-union organizing has been happening in the nonprofit sector — especially in universities and nonprofits with progressive missions. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Noah Smith recently accused graduate-student labor-union activists of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/06a91e5c-4c5c-4892-b077-f10e5f51b420?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">effectively LARPing as working class</a><span>. I’m not sure I would put it that way. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But I do think it’s relevant that they aren’t organizing against the interests of a capital-owning class — they’re fighting an internecine battle about the distribution of resources inside the university. These different stakeholders are then aligned with each other when you turn to a topic like whether there should be more subsidies to universities, something that all different kinds of university employees can agree on. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think that one reason the kind of rich-versus-poor politics that progressives want to meme into being struggles to get off the ground is that many policy conflicts pit one economic sector against another rather than the poor against the rich.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s normal to have conflicts in any workplace between management and rank-and-file workers (though </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b8b9987a-bf16-482d-a238-57d80e2210ac?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">most Americans like their boss</a><span>), but when Ford and G.M. object to regulations requiring electric vehicles, the U.A.W. is on their side. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Not only is the American labor market more complicated than “workers versus owners,” but within the category of “workers,” most people have at least </span><em>some</em><span> valuable specialized skills — they’re not just an undifferentiated mass of labor. People generally want the specific enterprise they work for to do well because if it expands, that gives them a shot at upward mobility, while if it does layoffs, they will find some of their specific experience devalued. And they definitely want their </span><em>occupation</em><span> to prosper. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Inequality without dichotomies </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That’s all just to say that the American economy is a land of contrasts. Or, it’s complicated. The point, I think, is that if you’re looking for a modern-day equivalent that will track the divide between gentry and peasants, you’re not going to find it. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Marx’s observations about the difference between people who own the means of production and the people who hire out their labor to the owners of capital goods resonate somewhat. But relatively few people fall on one side or the other of a stark divide. Most people own at least a little slice of the financial capital in the United States, and an even larger share of the rich and powerful corporate decision-makers in America are in fact working. Lots of people aren’t working for capitalist business enterprises at all. Beyond the government and nonprofit workers we talked about, lots of people are self-employed or work for small shops. Most poor people don’t have full-time jobs, and most people living off investment income are retired people who spent their prime years working. </p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up political analysis because it probably tracks some underlying psychological traits that are politically relevant. But there are big, well-known gaps within the education system. There’s a huge difference between attending Yale and attending Southern Connecticut State University, which is just two miles to the north. In particular, as college attendance has expanded, merely having a degree from somewhere or other has become less and less an elite credential. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I don’t think any of this is particularly surprising or controversial. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it does mean that all statements of the form “the real class divide in America is such-and-such” are going to fail. I don’t want to say something like “there is no class in America” because that would sound like I’m denying there is inequality in America when you can easily look it up and see that there’s a lot. You can look at the top 1 percent or top 10 percent or top 0.001 percent or you can compare the median to the </span><em>bottom</em><span> 10 percent, and these are all very different measures and they all show an unequal society. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’m just saying the modern economy is too large and complicated to characterize as a simple workers-versus-owners dichotomy. And in terms of social attitudes, it’s not shameful or suspect to be upwardly mobile or cross class lines. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">College versus non-college does track a big difference in political behavior, but my guess is that’s because it tracks psychological attitudes rather than specific economic roles. When you take a weird edge case like Platner, who got into a selective school but then dropped out, you get a guy with normal millennial college-graduate political views and a standard base of electoral support for someone with those views.</p><p class="button-wrapper"
